issues.legal_issue: An ex parte review decision made after notice was served and the affected person failed to appear did not violate natural justice.
material_facts: The Collector served the landowner with notice that the earlier surplus-area decision might be reviewed.
The landowner did not appear, and the Collector proceeded ex parte.
issues.conclusion: The ex parte review decision did not violate the principles of natural justice.
issues.legal_principle: A person who has been served with notice and an opportunity to attend cannot establish a denial of natural justice merely because the decision was made ex parte after that person failed to appear. The Court relied on the Collector’s recorded recital that notice had been served; it cited no earlier case for this point.

predicates.land_surplus_review_proceeding: An authority reviewed a decision determining whether a landowner had surplus land.
predicates.notice_served: The authority served the affected person with notice of the proposed review.
predicates.recipient_failed_to_appear: The person who received notice did not attend the proceeding.

issues.definition: When a land-surplus review proceeds after notice is served and the recipient does not appear, the ex parte decision does not, on those facts alone, violate natural justice.

issues.legal_issue: The permissible holding under the applicable land-ceiling definition was limited to the ordinary-acre ceiling where the standard-acre conversion exceeded that ceiling.
material_facts: The statutory definition provided for thirty standard acres, but applied a sixty-ordinary-acre limit where conversion of thirty standard acres exceeded sixty ordinary acres.
The landowner held 93.80 ordinary acres, and the Collector’s earlier decision had treated the permissible limit as thirty standard acres.
issues.conclusion: The applicable permissible limit was sixty ordinary acres, and the earlier no-surplus decision was based on a mistaken understanding of that limit.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(2) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act defined permissible area as thirty standard acres, subject to a limit of sixty ordinary acres where conversion of thirty standard acres exceeded sixty ordinary acres.

predicates.land_ceiling_proceeding: An authority determined the permissible holding and surplus land of a landowner.
predicates.standard_area_conversion_exceeds_ordinar: Conversion of the stated standard-acre allowance into ordinary acres would exceed the applicable ordinary-acre limit.

issues.definition: In a land-ceiling proceeding, where conversion of the standard-acre allowance exceeds the ordinary-acre limit, the permissible area is limited by the ordinary-acre ceiling.

issues.legal_issue: A review application made outside the prescribed review period without an explanation for the delay was prima facie time-barred.
material_facts: Section 24 of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act applied the appeal, review, and revision provisions of sections 80 to 84 of the Punjab Tenancy Act, 1887, so far as applicable.
Section 82 of the Punjab Tenancy Act prescribed ninety days for a review application, with an extension available on sufficient cause.
Even accepting the date on the uncertified copy of the application as accurate, the application was made about three and a half years after the order, and it gave no reason for the delay.
issues.conclusion: The review application was prima facie time-barred, and the revision could be rejected on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 24 of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act and section 82 of the Punjab Tenancy Act, 1887, a review application had to be made within ninety days; the period could be enlarged if sufficient cause for the delay was shown. The Court found no explanation for the delay and treated the application as prima facie time-barred.

predicates.land_ceiling_review_proceeding: A party sought review of an order made in a land-ceiling proceeding.
predicates.review_application_outside_prescribed_wi: The party applied for review after the applicable review period had expired.
predicates.no_sufficient_cause_shown: The party did not show sufficient cause for failing to apply within the applicable period.

issues.definition: A review application in a land-ceiling proceeding is time-barred when it is made after the applicable period and the applicant shows no sufficient cause for the delay.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge to the Collector’s authority to review an earlier order based on the order having been made by a predecessor was not established when that factual basis was not alleged.
material_facts: The landowner argued that the Collector could not review the earlier order because it had probably been made by the Collector’s predecessor.
Neither the writ petition nor the appeal grounds alleged that the earlier order had been made by a different person.
issues.conclusion: The contention that the Collector lacked authority to review the earlier order was rejected because the asserted factual basis was not alleged.
issues.legal_principle: The Court rejected the contention on the record before it because it had not been alleged that the earlier order was made by someone other than the officer who later reviewed it. The Court cited no earlier case for this point.

predicates.land_ceiling_review_proceeding: An authority reviewed an earlier decision made in a land-ceiling proceeding.
predicates.prior_decision_by_different_officer_not_: The challenger did not allege that the earlier decision had been made by a different officer.

issues.definition: In a land-ceiling review proceeding, a challenge based on the earlier decision having been made by a different officer is unsubstantiated when that fact was not alleged.

issues.legal_issue: A writ challenge alleging that land was wrongly included in a surplus-area calculation could not succeed without authentic supporting records where the land classification remained disputed.
material_facts: The landowner asserted that more than twenty bighas of banjar and ghairmumkin land had been included in calculating the surplus area.
The landowner provided no survey-number particulars or relevant Jamabandi or Khasra Girdawari extracts to establish the land’s classification.
The classification issue therefore remained disputed, and the High Court dismissed the writ petition in limine.
issues.conclusion: The High Court rightly dismissed the writ petition in limine because the landowner had not provided authentic proof of the asserted land classification.
issues.legal_principle: A factual claim about land classification cannot be established in a writ proceeding by assertion alone where authentic supporting records are absent and the fact remains disputed. The Court noted that the Commissioner had referred to Nemi Chand v. State and the Financial Commissioner’s ruling in Jiwan Singh v. Amrik Singh, but it resolved the challenge on the absence of proof and the time-barred review application rather than adopting those rulings.

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenging_surplus_: A party sought writ relief against a determination of surplus land.
predicates.land_classification_claim_unsupported_by: The party did not provide reliable records supporting the claimed classification of the land.
predicates.land_classification_remains_disputed: The parties or the record left the land’s classification as a disputed factual matter.

issues.definition: A land-classification challenge to a surplus determination cannot succeed in a writ proceeding when authentic supporting records are absent and the classification remains disputed.
